jlc.title: Markup vs. Margin
jlc.author: Sal Alfano
confirms: If we have $1,000 in direct costs, our markup is set at $500, thus equaling a total selling price of $1,500.
Therefore, a 50% markup is equivalent to a 33% margin.
So, a 100% markup gives a 50% margin.
If you'd like to earn a 50% margin on your next project, you must double the direct cost amount to achieve it.

xero.title: Margin vs markup
confirms: a 50% markup actually gives you a 33.3% margin.
Margin measures profit as a percentage of revenue (the selling price); markup measures it as a percentage of cost.
Gross margin only accounts for the direct cost of goods sold. It does not include rent, salaries, utilities, marketing, or other operating expenses.

priceOverMarkup.note: the 500 is one third of the 1,500 price

targetPriceUsd.note: Price = Cost / (1 - margin), rearranged from Xero's margin formula: margin = (price - cost) / price, so price = cost / (1 - margin)

targetMarginCheckPct.note: the worked example lands on exactly a 40% margin

targetMarkupPct.note: Xero's conversion Markup = Margin / (1 - Margin) agrees: a 66.7% markup on 1,000 is 1,666.67
